opti-1: In 1872, an artist painted a wild canyon in Yellowstone.
opti-2: That year, Yellowstone became the world's first national park.
opti-3: Bison had almost disappeared. Inside the park, they were safe.
opti-4: A whole park? Just for nature?
opti-5: Far away in Florida, a spoonbill flies over the Everglades.
opti-6: Zoom out. It lives in a river of grass, up to 60 miles wide.
opti-7: So why do people work so hard to protect wild places like this?
25-01-welcome: Our film starts with a painting from 1872 and ends in a river of grass. First, inspect some striped shells.
25-01-lesson: Today you're a park scientist. Watch a gator save the day, test two food webs, then dive down a reef.
25-01-check: Three quick questions. It's not graded. It's just for you, so give each one your best try.
25-01-assign: Time to show what you learned. Sort some actions, then tell us whether wild land is worth protecting.
how-25-01-specimen: Press Inspect specimen. Move the magnifying lens over the shells, then tap three things you notice.
how-25-01-compare: Put the scissors under one tray and the fence under the other: drag them, or tap one, then a tray. Press Run the test. Then swap.
how-25-01-wall: First, make a prediction. Then brush the glowing stop: drag across it (or tap it again and again) until the place shows.
how-25-01-det: Pick three parks, one at a time. Tap a clue, then pick its habitat. Predict a living thing you'll find, and watch it appear.
how-25-01-partc: Draw a national park scene with at least two zones, like a marsh and a forest. Label a living thing in one zone, and one action that protects it.
